facts.text: A deceleration limit specifies how hard a machine must or may slow down; regulators express these limits in several ways that are not directly comparable.
facts.quote: A deceleration limit is a rule about how hard a machine must, or may, slow down, and regulators write such rules in several different and not directly comparable ways.

facts.text: ISO 3450:2011 prescribes maximum stopping distances by machine type for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines with top speeds of at least 20 km/h.
facts.quote: ISO 3450:2011, for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines with top speeds of 20 km/h or more, prescribes maximum stopping distances by machine type

facts.text: ISO 3450:2011 measures stopping distance from brake-control actuation to standstill in the worst-case load configuration and summarizes performance as mean deceleration using a = v² / (2d).
facts.quote: measured from brake-control actuation to standstill in the worst-case load configuration, and summarizes performance as a mean deceleration from `a = v^2 / (2d)`.

facts.text: New South Wales guidance proposes minimum mean net decelerations of 0.60 m/s² for service brakes in service and 0.30 m/s² for secondary brakes, rising to 0.75 and 0.40 m/s² respectively for type testing, with grade and mass corrections. These values are a proposal, not an adopted rule.
facts.quote: The New South Wales guidance proposes a minimum mean net deceleration of 0.60 m/s² for service brakes in service (0.30 for secondary brakes), raised to 0.75 and 0.40 for type testing, with grade and mass corrections. It is a proposal, not an adopted rule.

facts.text: The US mining rule 30 CFR 56.14101, Table M-1, assumes constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s² (about 2.94 m/s²), system response time of 0.5–2.5 seconds depending on weight class, and 1 second of operator time.
facts.quote: The US mining rule (30 CFR 56.14101, Table M-1) assumes a constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s², about 2.94 m/s², plus a system response time of 0.5 to 2.5 s by weight class and 1 s of operator time

facts.text: US mining rule 30 CFR 56.14101 requires brakes capable of stopping and holding the loaded machine on the steepest grade the machine travels.
facts.quote: requires brakes that can stop and hold the loaded machine on the steepest grade it travels.

facts.text: The South African MOSH specification sets emergency-stop decelerations of 1.9 m/s² for machines faster than 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for other machines, and controlled-stop decelerations of 1.0 or 0.5 m/s².
facts.quote: The South African MOSH specification sets emergency-stop decelerations of 1.9 m/s² for machines faster than 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for others, controlled-stop decelerations of 1.0 or 0.5 m/s²

facts.text: The South African MOSH specification requires no wheel lock and limited veer, with testing performed unloaded on gradients of 1 percent or less.
facts.quote: no wheel lock and limited veer, tested unloaded on gradients of 1 percent or less [Chapter 7].

facts.text: UN Regulation No. 152 requires road cars to have a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s²; this is a minimum demand, not a measured deceleration.
facts.quote: UN Regulation No. 152 for road cars requires a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s²: a floor, and a demand rather than a measured deceleration [Chapter 8].

facts.text: No published maximum automatic-braking deceleration for earth-moving machines was found.
facts.quote: No published maximum automatic-braking deceleration for earth-moving machines was found

facts.text: ISO 21815 leaves the automatic-braking intervention profile to the machine manufacturer.
facts.quote: ISO 21815 leaves the intervention profile to the machine manufacturer [Chapter 8].

facts.text: US rule FMVSS No. 127 treats a false activation as a failure if peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more; this is the on-road ceiling quoted by the booklet.
facts.quote: The one on-road ceiling the booklet quotes is in the US rule FMVSS No. 127, where a false activation fails if peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more [Chapter 3].

facts.text: The booklet recommends commanding deceleration as a_command = min(a_need, a_traction, a_stability, a_machine, a_load), with a jerk-limited ramp.
facts.quote: The booklet's recommended rule is to command the minimum of several limits, `a_command = min(a_need, a_traction, a_stability, a_machine, a_load)`, ramped with a jerk limit

facts.text: The booklet recommends holding automatic braking after the stop and releasing it only on operator action where rollaway is possible.
facts.quote: held after the stop, and released only on operator action where rollaway is possible [Chapter 8].

facts.text: Minimum-deceleration requirements tell the collision-mitigation program how little deceleration the program may assume.
facts.quote: The floors tell the program how little deceleration it may assume

facts.text: Because no published automatic-braking deceleration ceiling was found, the program must derive a safe maximum for each machine family through stability and traction analysis and tests.
facts.quote: the missing ceiling means the safe maximum must be derived per machine family from stability and traction analysis and tests [Chapter 8].

facts.text: Before pooling braking sources, the program must convert the sources to one stopping-distance definition and one time origin because the sources mix definitions.
facts.quote: Because the sources mix definitions, the program must convert them to one definition of stopping distance and one time origin before pooling them [Chapter 8].
